questions.question: Read the passage on human rights, then answer: what do all human beings deserve?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** All human beings deserve **equal right to a decent existence and proper development**.

**What the passage says.**

> "All human beings deserve equal right to a decent existence and proper development."

**The two ideas in the phrase.** "Decent existence" is the right to the conditions of a civilised life — food, shelter, health, work; "proper development" is the right to grow as a person — education, freedom of thought, participation in government. The rest of the passage merely lists the instruments by which these two are protected.

questions.question: What can the laws of a country do for its people?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The laws of a country **protect the rights of individuals belonging to any race, religion, sex, colour or caste**, and ensure that **they are not discriminated against on those grounds**.

**What the passage says.**

> "Most countries have laws protecting the rights of individuals belonging to any race, religion, sex, colour or caste and ensuring that they are not discriminated against on those grounds."

**Suggesting the answer in the paper.** The question is deliberately broad; the fairest short answer is the one above, with a one-line illustration — e.g. a law against refusing a house or a job because of caste — to show that the protection is practical.

questions.question: With what purpose was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The purpose of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is **to protect the human rights of citizens** — to secure for every person, in every member state, the rights it lists.

**What the passage says.**

> "The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10th December 1948 by the General Assembly. All the member states are expected to protect the human rights of their citizens."

**Background that earns the extra mark.** The Declaration was adopted in the shadow of the Second World War and the Holocaust; its thirty articles set out civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights as a common standard for all nations, and member states are expected to make them part of their own law.

questions.question: What is the right of life?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The right of life is **the right to life in freedom of thoughts, speech, and to take part in governments, education, work — and not to be discriminated against on these grounds**.

**What the passage says.**

> "The rights included in the declaration are right to life, liberty and security of person, freedom of thoughts, religion, peaceful assembly, right to take part in the government, right to work, education and leisure."

**How to put it in the paper.** "The right to life means the right to live with liberty and security of person — not merely to exist, but to think, speak, worship, assemble, work, learn and take part in the government of one's country without discrimination."

questions.question: What are the rights included in the Declaration?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The rights included in the Declaration are the **right to life, liberty and security of person; freedom of thoughts and religion; peaceful assembly; the right to take part in the government; the right to work, education and leisure**. The Declaration has **thirty articles**, which include civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.

**What the passage says.**

> "This Declaration has 30 articles, which include civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. For example, right to life, liberty and security of person, freedom of thoughts, religion, peaceful assembly, right to take part in the government, right to work, education and leisure."

**Extra point.** The constitutions of democratic countries include most of these rights; in India some civil and political rights are guaranteed as **Fundamental Rights**, while the **Directive Principles of State Policy** list the important social and economic rights.

questions.question: Find words in the passage which mean the same as the following: (i) take care (para-1) (ii) freedom (para-2).
questions.answer:
**Answer.** (i) take care — **ensuring**; (ii) freedom — **liberty**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "...and **ensuring** that they are not discriminated against on those grounds." (para 1)

> "right to life, **liberty** and security of person..." (para 2)

**Note.** Give the exact single word; "ensuring" must keep its *-ing* form as printed.

questions.question: On the basis of your reading of the passage on time, make notes on it using headings and sub-headings. Use recognizable abbreviations wherever necessary.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: The Value of Time**

1. **Nature of time**
   1.1 precious
   1.2 can be measured but not controlled
   1.3 limited for each of us
   1.4 lapse of time is never regained
   1.5 has wings; waits for none

2. **Importance of time**
   2.1 proper use gives a bright future
   2.2 work done at the right time is never unrewarded
   2.3 must be used carefully and properly
   2.4 should not be wasted in useless pursuits

3. **Effect of disregarding time**
   3.1 time will disappear
   3.2 time will neglect us and not help us
   3.3 time will be lost

4. **How to use time well**
   4.1 plan and estimate the time available
   4.2 estimate the work to be finished
   4.3 work at the accurate/right time
   4.4 avoid wandering here and there

5. **The saying**
   5.1 "we can wait for a man, money and time of course, but time and tide waits for none"

**Key to abbreviations.** abbr. – abbreviations; est. – estimate; b/c – because; dep. – depends; acc. – accurate; i.e. – that is.

questions.question: Write a summary of the passage on time in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Time is precious. It can be measured but not controlled, so we should use it carefully and properly and not waste it in useless pursuits. The one who does not honour time is neglected by time itself. Time has wings; a lapse of time is never regained. Work done in the right direction at the right time can never go unrewarded, so we must plan our time, estimate how much time we have and how much work we must finish within it. Proper use of time alone can give us a bright future.

**Word count.** About 100 words. Keep the order — value, warning, method, result — which is the order of the passage.

questions.question: You have lost your cell phone in your school. Give details of the cell phone and the probable day you lost it. Your description should be fit for the 'Lost and Found' notice board of your school.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**ABC SCHOOL — NOTICE**

**LOST AND FOUND**

*May 11, 2020*

I am Rahul of class XII. I lost my **cell phone** in our **school playground during our extra-curricular class** yesterday, the 10th of May.

The phone is a **new One Plus 7T Pro, in onyx black colour**, with a black cover and a small scratch on the back panel. I am requesting you that if anyone has found my phone please give it to the undersigned in our school office room. A suitable reward will be given.

**Rahul**
12th Student

**Format points.** A "Lost and Found" notice names the article, gives **identifying marks** (model, colour, cover, damage), states the **probable place and time of loss**, tells the finder what to do, and is signed with the name and class — within 50 words.

questions.question: You are the head boy of a +2 school, Ramgarh. Write a notice for the school notice board inviting students for a trip to Goa, giving detailed information to the students.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**ABC SCHOOL, RAMGARH — NOTICE**

*May 15, 2018*

**TRIP TO GOA**

Our school is organising a trip to **Goa from May 20–26, 2018** for students of classes **XI and XII**. The trip includes visits to the local **beaches, churches, museums and markets**. The students will be accompanied by **four teachers**. The cost of the trip, inclusive of travel, boarding and lodging, will be **twelve thousand per student**.

Interested students should submit the **parents' consent slip, medical fitness certificate and the money** to the undersigned by **6 May**.

**Tom**
Head Boy

**Format points.** The institution, the word NOTICE, the date, the destination and dates, the class eligibility, the itinerary, the cost, the supervisors, and what the student must submit **and by when**.

questions.question: You are a reporter of *The Hindustan Times*. Report about a road accident involving a bus and a car, including details of the number of people injured, in not more than 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**TWO INJURED AS BUS RAMS CAR NEAR KANKE**

*By a Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 20 February 2020.** Two persons were injured, one of them seriously, when a private bus rammed a car on the Kanke Road near the Pandra crossing this morning.

According to the police, the Ranchi–Patna bus was coming at speed from the Gandhi Nagar side when the driver lost control on the wet road and hit the car standing near the crossing. The car was crushed on the driver's side; its driver, identified as Rajesh Kumar of Kanke, and a passenger were pulled out by local people and rushed to the RIMS trauma centre. The conductor of the bus also received minor injuries. The bus driver fled from the spot, and a case of rash and negligent driving has been registered against him at the Kanke police station.

**Format points.** A news report of an accident answers **what, where, when, how many, how and what next** in the first two paragraphs; the police and hospital details give it the authority of a report.

questions.question: Your school celebrated the 150th birth anniversary of M. K. Gandhi on 2nd October 2019. Write a report in 125 words to be published in your school magazine.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**150TH BIRTH ANNIVERSARY OF MAHATMA GANDHI CELEBRATED**

*Staff Reporter*

**Ranchi, 2 October 2019.** XYZ School celebrated the 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi on its campus.

On the occasion the programme started by **lighting the lamp and garlanding Gandhi's photograph**. On this special occasion of Gandhi Jayanti, in order to make the whole world aware of the great values like **non-violence, truth and religion** among the young, the school organised various programmes. While presenting the various principles of the father of the nation, a **dance performance and a music performance** were held.

The Principal said that as a source of inspiration for the world, XYZ School has decided to organise various programmes to commemorate Mahatma Gandhi from **2 October to 11 January**, so that everyone learns to make his country beautiful and clean. In this series a **film on Gandhi**, based on the life of the father of the nation, will be shown to the students.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the sequence of the function, the speech summarised in the third person, and the follow-up programme that makes the report more than a diary entry.

questions.question: Write a letter to the Editor of a newspaper in 125 words complaining about the frequent voltage fluctuation and low-voltage power supply in your area. You belong to a village in Ranchi district.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Indra Mohan Nagar**
**Ranchi district**
**18 February 2020**

The Editor
*The Hindustan Times*
Ranchi

**Subject: Regarding frequent breakdown of electricity**

Respected Sir

I would like to draw the kind attention of the concerned authorities, through the columns of your esteemed daily, to the fact that there is **frequent breakdown of electricity** in Indra Mohan Nagar, Damoh. The people of this colony are facing great difficulty because of it. The water supply is also connected with the electricity supply, so if there is uncertain breakdown of electricity its result can be seen on the water supply: the flow of our taps slows down and people get less quantity of water.

Students who are preparing for their examinations face great difficulty because of it; they are unable to make their study plan. The patients who are getting their treatment in different hospitals also face many difficulties, because their operations are not taking place on time. The number of thefts is multiplying, since the darkness of night gives thieves an easy chance.

I therefore request the concerned authorities to look into the matter and take necessary action.

Yours faithfully
**Ritwik**

**Format points.** Name the fault, show its **chain of effects** (power → water → study → hospital → crime), and close with a specific request.

questions.question: You are Sandhya/Somra. You bought a scooter of a reputed brand from Bonda Motor Company, Ranchi. After a month it started giving trouble. Write a letter to the dealer asking him to replace it with a new scooter.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Sandhya/Somra**
Ranchi
February 12, 2019

Bonda Motor Company
Ranchi

**Subject: Replacement of scooter**

Dear Sir

Last month I purchased a **scooter** of your reputed brand from your showroom, and I got it parked in my parking area. But I find that the scooter doesn't work at all. The local mechanic whom I consulted examined it many times at my request and says that there is a **problem in the engine**. He has advised me to communicate with your scooter service centre and tell them to check the scooter, and he says that if it is a big problem in the engine I should ask for the scooter to be replaced.

So, sir, I request you to **replace my scooter** as soon as possible. Because of the scooter I cannot manage my whole day's work; it is impossible for me to go on even for a day without it. I request you to replace the scooter immediately under the terms and conditions of the deal. I hope you would appreciate my problems and effect the replacement at your earliest.

Thanking you
Yours faithfully
**Raja**

**Format points.** The letter gives the date of purchase, the **fault as diagnosed by a mechanic**, the **consequence** for the buyer, and a clear request for replacement under the warranty. Keep the dealer's name and the buyer's address consistent.

questions.question: You are worried about the hike in the prices of essential commodities like gas, pulses and vegetables. Write an article on this in about 150 words for publication in a local daily, suggesting certain steps to curb price hike.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**HIKE IN THE PRICES OF ESSENTIAL COMMODITIES**

Price is ever on the increase. A rise in price, economists say, is a sign of development and prosperity. But during the last two decades prices of almost all the essential commodities have been increasing at an alarming rate. These soaring prices have caused great unrest and frustration among the people. The people belonging to the middle class and the salaried people are hit hard.

There are many causes of the unprecedented rise in prices — **inflation, black marketing, hoarding, a faulty credit system, over-population and improper distribution**. Shopkeepers should be directed to **display the stock of essential commodities along with their prices**. Those who buy and sell in the black market should be punished, and the production of food should be increased.

Let us hope that the government will be able to bring down the soaring prices. What is needed is the right intention and the force of will. The government has, in the recent past, taken some steps to control the prices and revamp the economy of the country; these efforts have met with partial success and inflation has been controlled to some extent.

**Format points.** An article on prices begins with the facts, explains the **causes**, suggests **practical remedies** and ends on a note of cautious hope — do not merely complain.

questions.question: Write an article in about 150 words on the topic 'Need of Communal Harmony'.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**NEED OF COMMUNAL HARMONY**

Integrity refers to working in unity and harmony with everyone. One contrary to it is not supporting the bad or harmful actions by anyone. When someone achieves success the only keyword that surrounds him is his **hard work and truthfulness** — not his community.

We live in a country which is diverse in nature. India is the only country where people of many religions live in the same place in peace. However, there are several social divisions which often lead to crisis and war in our country. People should not keep themselves above others due to their high economic conditions or social status, but should rather stay integrated and help one in need with respect. We should show integrity by following the laws and rules laid down by our government and respect its decisions for the welfare of our country, which, if broken, will lead to parting our own country or people.

Therefore, we should not practise any kind of discrimination with anyone on the basis of caste, religion, status and so far. Hence our nation's prosperity is associated with integrity, and we should respect each and every one.

**Format points.** Define the idea, give its **national importance** with the Indian example, name the danger of division, and end with a duty owed by the ordinary citizen.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: 'Fisherman in the harm cold sea / Would not harm whales / And the man gathering salt / Would look at his hurt hand.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **Keeping Quiet**; poet — **Pablo Neruda**.

**Context.** These lines come in the middle of the poem, where the poet imagines the effect of a deliberate silence. The fisherman in the "harm cold sea" would stop harming the whales, and the salt-gatherer would look at his own hurt hands. In the quiet moment each worker would see what his work is doing — to the world and to himself.

questions.question: What would the fisherman do?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The fisherman **would not harm the whales**. In the still moment he would leave the whales alone and stop his killing.

**Note.** The booklet prints "Fisherman are looking at their hurt hands" here, which repeats the answer to part (c) and is wrong: the passage's own words are "Fisherman in the cold sea / Would not harm whales". The hurt hands belong to the *salt-gatherer*, not the fisherman — keep the two parts separate in the answer sheet.

questions.question: What would the salt gathering man do?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The salt-gathering man **would look at his hurt hands**, which the salt has cracked and burned.

**Explanation.** He gathers salt with his own hands, and the brine has hurt them badly, but in the day's rush he never notices. The silence of the poem gives him the one thing he lacks — time to see his own body and his own labour.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: 'Far from the gusty waves these children's faces / Like rootless weeds, their hair torn round their pallor; / The tall girl with her weighed-down head.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum**; poet — **Stephen Spender**.

**Context.** These opening lines describe the children of a slum classroom: faces "far from the gusty waves", "like rootless weeds", hair "torn round their pallor", and a tall girl with her "weighed-down head". The images present children who are starved, neglected and without any root in a secure world.

**Syllabus note.** The chapter is **outside the current syllabus** (deleted text) but the extract survives in older question banks.

questions.question: Whom does the poet call 'rootless weeds'?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet calls the **slum children** "rootless weeds". Their faces, pale and neglected, grow unwanted like weeds, with no home, care or future.

**Explanation.** A weed is a plant nobody plants and nobody tends, and it is pulled out without regret. Spender's simile says that these children exist in the same insecure, unwanted way — hence "their hair torn round their pallor" and, later in the poem, "the paper-seeming boy, with rat's eyes".

questions.question: How does the poet describe the tall girl?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The poet says that the girl was sitting in the classroom **with her head weighed down**, which is due to **poverty and malnutrition**.

**Explanation.** The "tall girl with her weighed-down head" is one detail that carries the whole condition of the class. She is exhausted and anaemic, and her drooping head is the poem's image of a childhood bent under a burden it never chose.

questions.question: Why does Pablo Neruda want us to keep quiet? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Our life is **hasty and without direction**. The poet wants to say that we should keep ourselves away from wrong deeds and thinking for a while. **A long silence can soothe our feelings and help in removing our sadness.**

**Explanation.** In "Keeping Quiet" he asks us to count to twelve and "keep still", because "most of our troubles are due to our hurry and becoming rash". The silence would let the fisherman spare the whale and the salt-gatherer look at his hurt hands, and it would end the "sadness of never understanding ourselves". He adds at once that he does not want "total inactivity" or death — only a pause that renews life.

questions.question: What was the poet's childhood fear? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **The death after ageing** is the greatest fear of the poet's childhood. She realises that **her mother's face has become like the withered moon**; she has lost her charm and looks pale like that of a corpse.

**Explanation.** In Kamala Das's poem the sight of her dozing mother in the car brings back "the old familiar ache" — the child's fear of losing her mother, which is really the fear of death itself. She hides it by looking out at "young trees" and "merry children" and by smiling at the airport: "see you soon, amma".

questions.question: Describe Aunt Jennifer's fingers. (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Aunt Jennifer is **surrounded by the ordeals of her married life**. She finds her **heavy responsibilities** hard to pull with an ivory needle. The **heavy weight of her wedding ring** sits heavily upon her fingers that bonded her with the tradition.

**Explanation.** Adrienne Rich writes that "Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool / Find even the ivory needle hard to pull". The fluttering shows weakness and nerves; the "massive weight of Uncle's wedding band" is both a real ring and the marriage that has mastered her. Her only freedom is the bold tiger she stitches.

questions.question: According to John Keats, beauty will never pass into nothingness. How? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** A beautiful thing is **a source of internal joy**; its attraction grows with the passage of time. It provides us **mental peace** and its **impact never fades away**. Beautiful things dismiss the moment of sadness and fill our spirit with optimism and hope.

**Explanation.** Keats opens the poem with "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever: / Its loveliness increases; it will never / Pass into nothingness". The sun, the moon, the trees, the daffodils, the clear rills and the musk-rose each make "a bower quiet for us" and pour "some shape of beauty" into our "dark spirits" — and because each generation finds the same joy in them, beauty outlives the moment in which it is seen.

questions.question: What changes did the order from Berlin cause in the school that day? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** An **order from Berlin** was put up on the bulletin board. It said that **only German would be taught in the schools of Alsace and Lorraine**. Usually, when the school began, there was much noise and activity, and the noise could be heard in the street; **but that day there was unusual silence**.

**Explanation.** In "The Last Lesson" the order turns an ordinary school day into an occasion: M. Hamel wears his Sunday clothes, the village elders sit at the back, and the French lesson becomes the last one. The silence Franz notices at the gate is the mark of a whole people's loss.

questions.question: How did the crofter earn thirty kronor? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The crofter was no longer able to do day labour, so **it was his cow which supported him**. She gave milk for the **creamery every day**, and last month he had received all of **thirty kronor** in payment.

**Explanation.** In Selma Lagerlöf's "The Rattrap" the old man shows the peddler the three ten-kronor notes the creamery paid him and hides them in a leather pouch under a stone; the peddler steals them the next morning and is hunted through the forest until Edla's kindness at the Ramsjö ironworks gives him a chance to return them.

questions.question: Describe the miserable conditions of the ragpickers of Seemapuri. (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** In Seemapuri ragpickers live in large numbers. They live there **without an identity and permission**, though they have **ration cards** that enable them to vote and buy grain. They live in **structures of mud with a roof of tin and tarpaulin**; there is **no sewage, drainage or running water**. They lead a miserable life with no progress in their life.

**Explanation.** In Anees Jung's "Lost Spring" the settlement houses more than ten thousand people who came from Bangladesh in 1971. For them "food is more important" than identity, and garbage is "wrapped in wonder" because a rupee or a ten-rupee note may be hidden in it. The chapter's point is that this is a part of Delhi and yet "miles away" from it.

questions.question: Who was Rajkumar Shukla? Why did he meet Gandhi? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Rajkumar Shukla was a **peasant** — a poor sharecropper of Champaran. He met Gandhi because he wished that **Gandhiji would see the condition of the sharecroppers of Champaran**. He hoped that Gandhiji would solve the problems of the poor peasants of Champaran, who were being exploited by the British landlords.

**Explanation.** In "Indigo" Shukla is "illiterate but resolute": he meets Gandhi at the Lucknow Congress session, follows him to Cawnpore and Calcutta, and finally takes him by train to Patna. His persistence turns one peasant's grievance into the Champaran campaign, the first successful movement of civil disobedience in India.

questions.question: Why was Sophie jealous of her brother's silence? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sophie used to think that her brother had **seen a lot of places**, but she had not. Her brother **never talked to her about his visits to many places**, and therefore **she felt jealous of his silence**.

**Explanation.** In A. R. Barton's "Going Places" Sophie imagines that Geoff's silences are full of a wider experience — that people tell him things, that he has "been places". It is her own narrow world, the biscuit factory and the corner shop, that makes his quietness enviable, and she uses him as the audience for her invented meeting with Danny Casey.

questions.question: Why do most celebrity writers dislike being interviewed? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Most celebrity writers **see themselves as the victims of interviews**. They consider an interview **an unwarranted intrusion into their private lives**, and they feel that it somehow **diminishes them**.

**Explanation.** In Christopher Silvester's "The Interview", a chapter drawn from *The Penguin Book of Interviews*, the dislike is explained by the interview's peculiar power: what is said in a few careless minutes is printed as a settled opinion, and the interviewer, not the writer, decides what the reader sees. H. G. Wells called the interview "an affront", and Kipling thought it "immoral" and "a crime".

questions.question: Why do you think Gandhiji considered the Champaran episode to be a turning point in his life? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Gandhi considered the Champaran episode to be a **turning point**, because from now on the peasants came out of the fear of the Britishers. He had come to Champaran to visit Shukla for a few days, but after seeing the miserable conditions he **lived there for seven months**. The British landlords used to make the peasants cultivate indigo for them. But when Germany discovered synthetic indigo, the cultivation of indigo was stopped in India, as now the price of indigo would come down. This issue was moved into the court, where **Mr. Gandhi was declared the winner**. The peasants got a small part of money as compensation, and their **fear of the British was now shattered**.

**Why it mattered nationally.** The success meant the first victory of civil disobedience in India: the English landlords were forced to surrender part of the money and, with it, part of their prestige. Gandhi himself said that the amount of the refund was less important than the fact that the peasants had learnt they had rights and defenders — and that the movement had grown out of an attempt to remove the distress of poor people rather than out of defiance.

questions.question: In what conditions do the bangle makers of Firozabad live? Why can't they come out of the state of poverty? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Firozabad is famous for its bangle industry, but the factories are located in **stinking lanes choked with garbage**. The bangle makers work in **dingy rooms with no windows for fresh air**. Children also join their parents in bangle making: according to the writer, more than **20,000 children** are engaged in bangle making. They work along with their parents in the **glass furnace at high temperature**, and are exposed to various health hazards. **Most of them end up losing their eyesight before they become adults.**

The poor bangle workers are fallen in a **web of poverty**. They have fallen into a **vicious circle of sahukars, middlemen and the police**. These never allow the poor workers to organise a cooperative, so the bangle workers of Firozabad are confined to poverty and exploitation.

**Why the circle cannot be broken.** They have no savings to start a cooperative, no education to find other work, and no leader to speak for them; the fear of the police and of losing even the little they earn keeps them from combining. Anees Jung notes that their fathers' trade is the only future they are offered, and that a dream like Mukesh's — to be a motor mechanic — is almost an act of rebellion.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: Who was Geoff Green? What does the 'Student on Ice' programme aim to do? (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Geoff Green is the **founder and executive director of the 'Students on Ice' expedition**. The aim of this programme is **to take high school students to the ends of the world** and to provide them with **inspiring education opportunities** which will help them foster a new understanding and respect for our planet.

It has been in operation for six years now, headed by the Canadian **Geoff Green**, who got tired of "carting celebrities and retired, rich, curiosity-seekers" who could only "give" back in a limited way. With students on ice he offers the future generation of policy-makers a **life-changing experience at an age when they are ready to absorb, learn and, most importantly, act**.

**Why the programme exists.** In "Journey to the End of the Earth" Tishani Doshi travels with the expedition to Antarctica and sees how the sight of the continent's ice and wildlife changes the young travellers; Green's bet is that those who see the earth's past there will defend its future here.

questions.question: How did Bama learn about untouchability and the caste system? (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** One day while coming back from school Bama saw one of the elders of her community carrying a packet of some snacks for the landlord. The elder was **holding the packet in such a way as not to touch his body**, because it might be polluted. It was a funny thing for Bama. **On reaching home her elder brother told her that it was a case of untouchability**: the lower caste people must not touch upper caste people or their things, because it polluted them. It was then that Bama knew about the **social discrimination faced by her community**.

**What she saw.** The old man carried the packet by its string, "without touching it", and handed it to the landlord — a small daily humiliation that the child first found comic. Her brother Annam explained the custom, told her that the community had been kept ignorant for centuries, and said that **education was the only way out**: if she studied hard she could make her own way and would not have to bow before such rules. Bama took his advice, stood first in her class, and years later wrote the episode down.

questions.question: How was Derry's face burnt? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Derry was a boy of ten years. He got **acid on one side of his face**. **The acid burnt his face**, leaving that side scarred and disfigured.

**Explanation.** In Susan Hill's "On the Face of It" Derry tells Mr. Lamb that he wandered into an empty garden as a child and climbed over a wall; the acid was lying there, and it "burned" his face. People stare at him, and he has withdrawn into himself, until Mr. Lamb — who has a tin leg — makes him see that "it's all relative".

questions.question: Why did Yumi refuse to bring hot water for the wounded soldier? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Yumi was the **maid of Hana**. She was **afraid of keeping a white man in the house**, as it was a **punishable offence against the government**. So she refused to bring water.

**Explanation.** In "The Enemy" the servants of the house refuse to touch the wounded American prisoner, and Yumi, who had helped at the birth of the Sadaos' child, simply walks out rather than help an enemy. Hana has to wash the man herself — the moment at which the household's loyalty to the state is set against the doctor's duty to a dying man.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: What was Gondwana? What happened to it? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Gondwana was a **giant amalgamated southern supercontinent**, located roughly around the present-day **Antarctica**. Around the time when the **dinosaurs were wiped out** and the age of mammals got under way, the landmass was **forced to separate into countries**, shaping the globe much as we know it today.

**Explanation.** In Tishani Doshi's "Journey to the End of the Earth", Gondwana flourished for about 500 million years with a much warmer climate and a huge variety of flora and fauna, before humans had appeared. Its break-up pushed India northwards, raised the Himalayas and set the pattern of the world's climate.

questions.question: What was Charley's hobby? Where did he find Sam's letter? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Charley's hobby was **stamp collection**. Charley found **Sam's letter in the first-day cover** that was part of his stamp collection. The letter was addressed to Charley by Sam.

**Explanation.** In Jack Finney's "The Third Level" the letter is dated 18 July 1894 and is postmarked Galesburg, Illinois — a first-day cover that could not possibly exist. In it Sam, the psychiatrist, writes that he has found the third level and is living in the old, peaceful Galesburg; the stamp collection is thus the story's proof that the past is reachable, or at least that Charley's longing has been shared.

questions.question: How did the Dewan and his wife help the Tiger King in finding the hundredth tiger? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The Dewan was relieved to see a tiger that had been brought from the **People's Park in Madras**, and he kept it **hidden in his house**. At midnight the Dewan and his wife **dragged the tiger to the car** and drove it to the forest where the Maharaja was hunting, and with great difficulty pushed it out.

The old tiger wandered into the Maharaja's presence; the Maharaja shot the beast and the tiger fell to the ground.

**Explanation.** In Kalki's story the hundredth tiger is not shot dead at once — it merely faints from the shock, and the hunters leave it lying there. The Maharaja's tally of a hundred is thus satisfied by a tame park animal that was driven to him in a car, which makes the final irony sharper when a **wooden** toy tiger kills him.
